title: Google Books Week Review: Four Key Findings from Our Testing Journey on The Verge
body:
Google’s first wave of “Googlebook” laptops—branded devices from Dell, Lenovo, Asus, Acer and HP that ship with the company’s newly unveiled ChromeOS 2—has been under intensive hands‑on review for the past week. Early impressions suggest the hardware is solid, the software refinements are noticeable, and the ecosystem is beginning to feel cohesive enough to challenge the entrenched dominance of Windows‑based ultrabooks. Yet the experience also highlights a handful of lingering gaps that could dictate whether consumers and enterprises will adopt the platform at scale.

The first notable takeaway is the consistency of build quality across the five manufacturers. Dell’s XPS‑styled model, Lenovo’s ThinkPad‑inspired variant, Asus’s ZenBook‑type offering, Acer’s Swift‑class device, and HP’s Envy‑based laptop all meet premium standards, with aluminum chassis, high‑resolution displays and robust keyboards. Google’s hardware partners appear to have taken the OS’s lightweight nature seriously, avoiding the “budget‑only” perception that plagued earlier ChromeOS devices. Battery life, a traditional selling point for ChromeOS, is impressive across the board, with most units delivering 10‑plus hours of mixed‑use endurance, thanks in part to the OS’s efficient power management and the modest power draw of the ARM‑based processors in several models.

Software-wise, ChromeOS 2 brings a suite of upgrades that feel less like incremental patches and more like a strategic pivot. The new “Google Play Store for ChromeOS” now supports a broader range of Android apps, including many productivity tools that were previously unavailable on the desktop. Moreover, the integration of Linux (Beta) has been refined: container launch times are faster, and file‑system sharing between ChromeOS and Linux environments is more seamless, allowing developers to run code editors, IDEs and even lightweight server stacks without a dual‑boot setup. The updated Files app now supports network drives and external storage with drag‑and‑drop ease, a long‑awaited feature for power users.

Despite these advances, the testing also uncovered friction points that could hinder broader adoption. First, the reliance on cloud‑centric workflows remains a double‑edged sword. While most everyday tasks run smoothly offline, certain enterprise applications still demand native Windows binaries or heavy‑duty client software that ChromeOS cannot emulate reliably. Second, the performance ceiling of the entry‑level ARM chips becomes apparent when multitasking with multiple Android apps and a Linux container simultaneously; occasional lag spikes suggest that higher‑end Intel or AMD options may be necessary for demanding users. Finally, the learning curve for non‑technical consumers persists, especially around managing Linux containers and configuring Android app permissions, which could deter the less tech‑savvy demographic.

From a market perspective, Google’s strategy appears to be shifting from “budget Chromebook” to “premium laptop with a cloud‑first OS.” By partnering with established OEMs, Google leverages existing distribution channels and brand trust, while positioning ChromeOS 2 as a viable alternative for both education and enterprise sectors. The inclusion of robust security features—verified boot, frequent automatic updates, and built‑in ransomware protection—aligns with corporate IT requirements, potentially opening doors for bulk deployments in schools and businesses that have already standardized on Google Workspace.

Looking ahead, the success of the Googlebook lineup will hinge on how quickly the ecosystem can close the remaining gaps. Expanded native support for Windows applications via remote desktop or virtualization, continued performance improvements on ARM platforms, and clearer onboarding experiences for Linux users will be critical. If Google can sustain the momentum of hardware quality, software maturity, and ecosystem integration, the next generation of ChromeOS laptops could reshape the laptop market, offering a compelling, secure, and cloud‑centric alternative to traditional operating systems.
